title: When to see someone
hookLine: practice complements, never replaces, medical or psychological care

lines: IS THERE A DOCTOR IN THERE?
cards: Open the contacts on your phone and scroll. There's probably a pizza place in there, a plumber, someone from a trip whose last name you've forgotten. Is there a doctor?
A counselor? A number to call at three in the morning if things got very dark? If the honest answer is no, the search may have to start on a bad night, when searching is hardest.
A week on the honest part of practice ends with a very practical honesty: practice is good company, and it is not a doctor.

teach.b: First, the line. Practice complements care. It never replaces it.
A practice can sit beside therapy, medicine and a good doctor; it shouldn't stand in for them. Second, the old texts agree.

The Jewish sage Ben Sira, whose book is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles and in the Apocrypha of some Protestant ones, says, in the King James text: "Honour a physician with the honour due unto him for the uses which ye may have of him: for the Lord hath created him."
In the same chapter he tells the sick to pray, and also to make room for the physician. Both, not either.
In Islam, a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari reports the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying that God has not sent down a disease without also sending down its cure.
Some readers take it to mean that seeking treatment is part of faith, not a lack of it. Third, the when.
Yesterday's signs that don't pass when you stop. Low mood that settles in for weeks. Not being able to work, sleep or eat.
Any thought of harming yourself. Those are reasons to see someone, not to sit longer. In an emergency, call your local emergency number; in the US, you can call or text 988.

teach.h: A WEEK OF WHERE PRACTICE ENDS.
teach.b: Fourth, the week: the replication crisis, what held up, too many good results, mindfulness without ethics, mindfulness in schools, hard experiences, and now this.
A week of saying where practice ends, so you can trust it where it doesn't.

how: Meditation teachers and religious communities can encourage people who are struggling to see a doctor or counselor, and to keep practice and prayer alongside professional care rather than instead of it.

games.q: what does “when to see someone” mean?
o: waiting until a hard spell passes on its own before telling anyone
knowing when practice should step aside for a doctor or counselor
a weekly check-in with a meditation teacher about your progress

games.q: when to see someone: tap the pairs.
p: call or text in the US

games.q: for weeks your mood has stayed low, and sleep is falling apart. what do you do?
o: sit longer every day until it lifts.
see a doctor or counselor, and keep practicing alongside.
stop practicing and wait it out alone.
games.why: practice complements care, never replaces it. Ben Sira says pray and make room for the physician: both, not either.

practice: Ask quietly: if things got hard, who would I call? Let a face or a place come: a family doctor, a counselor someone once mentioned, a clinic near you, a crisis line.
If nothing comes, notice that without judging it; it only means there's one small job to do, and you can breathe with the question for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: When to see someone. When signs don't pass, mood stays low, or harm crosses your mind, practice steps aside for real care. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: care first. Practice is good company, and it is not a doctor. See you tomorrow.
